profiles.name: Juan Jose Martinez Vega
profiles.description: Juan Jose Martinez Vega (Chiguiro) was extradited from Colombia, tried, and convicted of FARC narcotics conspiracy; sentenced to 330 months federal prison plus a required English educational/vocational training program.
profiles.finding: DOJ and appellate records identify Chiguiro; no verified portrait.

profiles.name: Joshua Key
profiles.description:
Joshua Key, born in Guthrie, Oklahoma in 1978, enlisted in the United States Army in 2002 and was stationed at Fort Carson, Colorado. He served eight months in Iraq in 2003 as a combat engineer, taking part in what he has described as some two hundred raids on civilian homes. Returning to the United States on leave in November 2003, he did not go back, and on March 8, 2005 he entered Canada at Toronto, filing an asylum claim three days later.

His refugee claim was rejected by the Immigration and Refugee Board on October 20, 2006. He won an appeal in the Federal Court on July 4, 2008, which required the claim to be reheard, but received a second negative decision on July 30, 2010. In 2016 he was granted temporary permission to work and to receive government health care while his case continued to be reviewed. With the Canadian author Lawrence Hill he wrote The Deserter's Tale, an account of his service in Iraq and his decision to leave. He has been publicly documented living in Winnipeg, Manitoba.

Present residence and outstanding United States military status unverified: reporting through 2024 places him among the American war resisters still seeking the right to remain in Canada, but no recent official record has been found confirming his current residence or the status of any military case against him. He is recorded here as currently in exile on the assumption that he remains abroad.
profiles.finding: The Tyee and Lawrence Hill/author material identify deserter; theater production photos show actors and are not portraits of Key. Better individual photo still pending.

profiles.name: Carlos Gamarra-Murillo
profiles.description:
Carlos Gamarra-Murillo, age 54, U.S. citizen, worked as a weapons broker for FARC and was caught in an Immigration and Customs Enforcement sting in 2005. He had attempted to trade 4,400 pounds of cocaine for M-60 machine guns, grenade launchers, M-16 rifles, and other weapons in a $4 million deal with undercover agents in Tampa, Florida. Pleaded guilty in 2005; 300 months federal prison plus 3 years supervised release.

The Bureau of Prisons records his release from FCI La Tuna on July 18, 2025.
profiles.finding: Initial exact-name search yielded no verified portrait.

profiles.name: David Bunt
profiles.description:
David Bunt was a U.S. Army private whose experience on deployment in Afghanistan led him to conclude that he could not in conscience kill another person. After rejection of his conscientious-objector application, he pleaded guilty at a Fort Bragg court-martial to missing a parachute jump and received a 45-day brig sentence. He began confinement at Camp Lejeune on September 22, 2004. Nuclear Resister’s January 2005 issue confirms that he had been released, but does not give the actual release date.

Sources: https://media.nukeresister.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/NR135_20041015small.pdf#page=2 ; https://media.nukeresister.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/NR135_20041015small.pdf#page=3 ; https://media.nukeresister.org/wp-content/uploads/resister/nr136.pdf#page=3
profiles.finding: Army Anniston director David Bunt and Navy Captain David R. Bunten are unlinked namesakes, rejected; no verified portrait.

profiles.name: Mohammed Mosharref Hossain
profiles.description:
Mohammed Mosharref Hossain was the Bangladeshi-American owner of an Albany, New York pizzeria and a founder of the Masjid As-Salam mosque in Albany. He was arrested on August 6, 2004 in an FBI sting operation in which informant Shahed Hussein, posing as an arms dealer, offered him a $50,000 cash loan to be repaid in $45,000 of pizza-shop business checks, with the loaned money allegedly proceeds from the sale of a Chinese surface-to-air missile to Jaish-e-Mohammed for use against the Pakistani Ambassador in New York. Hossain pulled imam Yassin Aref into the transaction solely as a religious witness.

He was convicted in October 2006 and sentenced in March 2007 to 15 years in federal prison. He was granted compassionate release in June 2020 because of advanced medical risk during the COVID-19 pandemic.
profiles.finding: Chron/Times Union caption identifies Hossain on right with Aref on left; group crop and rights review pending. Project SALAM sources found but current host serves Account Suspended.

profiles.name: Yassin Aref
profiles.description:
Yassin Aref is a Kurdish Iraqi imam who came to the United States as a UN refugee in 1999. He was the imam of Masjid As-Salam in Albany, New York at the time of his arrest on August 5, 2004 in an FBI sting operation. The FBI informant Shahed Hussein, posing as an arms dealer, asked pizzeria owner Mohammed Mosharref Hossain to launder money allegedly from the sale of a surface-to-air missile to Jaish-e-Mohammed; Aref was brought in solely as a religious witness to the loan transaction, in accordance with Islamic law on financial agreements.

He was convicted in October 2006 of conspiracy and money-laundering charges and sentenced in March 2007 to 15 years in federal prison. The 2023 ruling by U.S. District Judge Thomas McAvoy that the FBI informant Shahed Hussein had been a villain whose testimony in unrelated cases warranted relief came too late for Aref, who had already completed his sentence. He was deported to the Iraqi Kurdistan Region after release.
profiles.finding: Project SALAM 2013 press conference page identifies individual Loretto prison photograph; both projectsalam.org and yassinaref.com return Account Suspended on direct fetch. Prison group images identify subjects but not retrieved. WRMEA credits Will Waldron/Albany Times Union; follow-up pending.

profiles.name: Christopher Lay
profiles.description: Christopher Lay, age 20, son of Wade Lay, participated in the May 24, 2004 Tulsa bank-robbery attempt motivated by anti-federal-government grievance over the 1993 Waco siege. A bank security guard was killed. Convicted of first-degree murder and attempted robbery; sentenced to life in Oklahoma state prison.
profiles.finding: The Appeal detailed case report has photo illustration, not identified portrait. Air Force colonel and UC Irvine researcher namesakes rejected; Wade Lay photographs not Christopher.

profiles.name: Abdullah Webster
profiles.description: Sergeant Abdullah Webster, a Muslim convert from Houston, Texas, was an artillery noncommissioned officer with the 1st Infantry Division stationed in Schweinfurt, Germany. In 2004, when his unit was ordered to deploy to Iraq, he refused on the grounds that Islamic teaching forbade his participation in a war he understood as unjust against fellow Muslims; the Army refused his conscientious-objector application. He was court-martialed in Würzburg, Germany in June 2004, convicted of missing movement and disobeying orders, and sentenced to 14 months in military confinement, reduction to private, and a bad-conduct discharge. He served his sentence at the U.S. Army Confinement Facility in Mannheim, Germany.
profiles.finding: Courage to Resist profiles page explicitly identifies Webster image but only100x100 directory thumbnail; larger image pending. Visual artist namesake rejected.

profiles.name: Camilo Mejía
profiles.description: Staff Sergeant Camilo Mejía became the first U.S. soldier to publicly refuse to return to Iraq. After leading an infantry squad in Iraq for five months in 2003, he came home on leave and refused to redeploy, applying for conscientious-objector status on the grounds that he had witnessed war crimes including the use of small-arms fire as crowd control on civilians and the abuse of detainees at Al Asad airbase. The Army denied the application and court-martialed him at Fort Stewart, Georgia for desertion. He was convicted on May 21, 2004 and sentenced to one year in military prison; he served nine months at Fort Sill, Oklahoma. After his release he was elected national chairman of Iraq Veterans Against the War.
profiles.finding: Courage to Resist100x100 directory image found; Wikipedia current HTML has no portrait despite indexed caption. AWTT/Justseeds are artwork. ReadTheSpirit identifies deployment photograph, PBS discussion guide credits Camilo Mejia; larger source retrieval pending. Colombian photographer/multimedia/football namesakes rejected.

profiles.name: October Martinique Lewis
profiles.description:
October Martinique Lewis was part of the Portland Seven, a homegrown cell whose members studied books and films about jihad and also participated in firearms and militia training before 9/11. Lewis was the ex-wife of the group’s ringleader, Jeffrey Leon Battle. The group’s activities were discovered when a sheriff’s deputy in Washington state questioned several people as they held target practice. The FBI introduced informants, and they recorded the group talking about joining the Taliban by flying to China and then traveling to Afghanistan. Lewis wired money to Battle as part of his conspiracy to enter Afghanistan in October 2001 to fight with the Taliban. Lewis cooperated with authorities and received a lighter penalty.

Case characteristics: FBI sting operation, FBI confidential informant, cooperated with prosecutors. Organization referenced in charging documents: Taliban.
